title: The Wild Gallant
description: Dryden's first play, a prose comedy of intrigue performed before the court at Whitehall and a conspicuous failure that he later revised.
plot_or_argument: Lord Truceville pursues Lady Constance while pretending to be a wild gallant; a series of mistaken identities, a faked ghost, and an inn intrigue lead to a double marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts of low comedy and intrigue.
principal_characters: Lord Truceville; Lady Constance; Colonel Fairly; Bibber; Mrs Gripe; Set-Star; Mr Trice
meter_and_prosody: Predominantly prose.
historical_context: Performed by the Duke's Company at the Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields in February 1663 before Charles II and the court, who found it dull.
literary_significance: Dryden's dramatic debut; its failure taught him to move toward the rhymed heroic play, which he began with The Rival Ladies.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1669. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vols. XIII-XIV (California, 1992- ).

title: The Indian Queen
description: The first full English heroic play in rhymed couplets, set in the conquest of Mexico, written by Dryden in collaboration with his brother-in-law Sir Robert Howard.
plot_or_argument: The Aztec prince Acacis and the Indian hero Zempoalla are caught between love and ambition in the war against the Spaniards; Zempoalla's usurpation, the sacrifice of the captives, and the intervention of the gods lead to a final resolution.
narrative_structure: Five acts with masque-like spectacle, songs, and machinery.
principal_characters: Zempoalla; Acacis; Zempalla's son Amexia; Montezuma; Traxalla; Garrucca; the High Priest of the Sun
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed heroic couplets in iambic pentameter.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Company at the Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields in January 1664 with music by Henry Purcell's teacher John Banister; the collaboration quarrel is recorded in the prefaces.
literary_significance: The founding work of the English heroic drama, and the occasion of the Dryden-Howard controversy over rhyme that led to An Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
attribution_notes: The 1664 quarto names Dryden and Howard jointly; modern attribution assigns the bulk to Dryden.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1664. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vols. IX-X (California).

title: An Essay of Dramatic Poesy
description: Dryden's foundational work of English dramatic criticism, a dialogue among four friends on a barge during the Second Dutch War in which the merits of the ancients and moderns, and of the French and English stages, are debated.
plot_or_argument: Crites defends the ancients; Eugenius defends the moderns; Lisideius argues for French regularity; Neander (Dryden's spokesman) defends the English drama's variety and life, arguing that rhyme may be natural to serious plays.
narrative_structure: A four-part dialogue with an opening narrative frame.
principal_characters: Crites; Eugenius; Lisideius; Neander
meter_and_prosody: Elegant argumentative prose, one of the earliest examples of a distinctively modern English critical prose style.
historical_context: Composed during 1666-8 and dedicated to Charles Howard, Earl of Dorset; it responds to the neoclassical controversy ignited by Corneille and the Académie française.
literary_significance: The first major work of English literary criticism and the text that established Dryden as the father of English criticism; its comparative method and generous assessment of Shakespeare were decisive for the later canon.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Dryden; the speaker Neander is Dryden's anagrammatic self-portrait.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1668. Standard edition: Of Dramatic Poesy and Other Critical Essays (George Watson, ed., Dent, 1962); The Works of John Dryden, vol. XVII (California, 1971).

title: The Tempest; or, The Enchanted Island
alternative_titles: The Tempest or The Inchanted Island
description: The Davenant-Dryden adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest, adding a second island inhabitant, Hippolito, a sister for Miranda, and extensive musical and spectacular material; it held the stage for over a century.
plot_or_argument: Prospero, exiled to the island, raises a tempest that wrecks the Neapolitans; the new plot gives Miranda a sister and adds Hippolito, a young man who has never seen a woman, with whom both sisters fall in love.
narrative_structure: Five acts with songs, dances, and machinery; about half Shakespeare's text is retained and the rest newly written.
principal_characters: Prospero; Miranda; Hippolito; Ariel; Ferdinand; Dorinda; Caliban; Trinculo; Stephano; Sycorax
meter_and_prosody: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
historical_context: First performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields on 7 November 1667; Davenant died in 1668 before publication, and Dryden wrote the preface.
literary_significance: The dominant version of The Tempest on the English stage from 1667 until the nineteenth century and a crucial document of Restoration Shakespeare adaptation; it inspired Purcell's semi-opera The Fairy-Queen tradition and Shadwell's operatic version of 1674.
attribution_notes: The 1674 quarto names Davenant and Dryden; the extent of each contribution is disputed, but Dryden's preface claims the greater part of the new material as Davenant's design.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1674. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vols. XI-XII (California); The Tempest, Davenant and Dryden adaptation (Christopher Spencer, ed., Scolar Press, 1979).

title: The Conquest of Granada
alternative_titles: The Conquest of Granada by the Spaniards
description: Dryden's heroic play in two parts on the Christian conquest of Moorish Granada in 1492, whose overweening hero Almanzor became the type of the Restoration hero of honour and love.
plot_or_argument: Almanzor, a free-lance warrior of boundless ambition, serves first the Moors then the Spaniards, loves Almahide, and is torn between love, honour, and freedom until the fall of Granada and the lovers' final recognition.
narrative_structure: Two parts of five acts each, with a masque and an epilogue; the plot interweaves the historical siege with the love story.
principal_characters: Almanzor; Almahide; Boabdelin; Lyndaraxa; Abdalla; Selin; Ferdinand; Isabella; the Duke of Arcos
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed heroic couplets at their most sonorous and rhetorical.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Company at the Theatre Royal in December 1670 and January 1671 and dedicated to the Duke of York; it was attacked by Buckingham in The Rehearsal and defended by Dryden in the Defence of the Epilogue.
literary_significance: The supreme example of the English heroic drama and the occasion of the most important Restoration quarrel over the form; Almanzor's rhetoric of boundless will anticipates the eighteenth-century sublime.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1672 in two parts. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vols. XI-XII (California).

title: Marriage à la Mode
description: Dryden's tragicomedy, dedicated to the Earl of Rochester, which joins a high heroic plot of usurpation and concealed royalty with a low prose comedy of cuckoldry and gallantry.
plot_or_argument: In Sicily, the usurped king's true son Polydamas is discovered and restored, while in the comic plot Rhodophil and Palamede pursue each other's wives and are undone by their own devices.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a double plot: heroic verse tragedy above and prose comedy below, ending in both a recognition and a set of marriages.
principal_characters: Polydamas; Leonidas; Amalthea; Palmyra; Rhodophil; Palamede; Doralice; Melantha; Selin
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed heroic couplets in the high plot and prose in the low plot.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1672 and published in 1673; Melantha's affectation of French fashions satirises the court's Francophilia.
literary_significance: The finest Restoration tragicomedy and Dryden's best comedy; Melantha is one of the great comic portraits of the period and the play remained a repertory favourite.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1673. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vol. XIII (California).

title: Aureng-zebe; or, The Great Mogul
description: Dryden's heroic play on the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb's succession struggle, notable for its more restrained hero and for Dryden's prefatory doubt about the value of rhyme.
plot_or_argument: The aged emperor Shah Abbas is suspected of loving his son Aureng-zebe's mistress Indamora; the prince's constancy and filial duty survive a rebellion by his brother Morat, and order is restored.
narrative_structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single main action and a rival brother subplot.
principal_characters: Aureng-zebe; Indamora; Shah Abbas; Morat; Nourmahal; Arban; Benducar
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed heroic couplets, with a looser and more conversational movement than in The Conquest of Granada.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676, dedicated to the Earl of Mulgrave; the prologue's complaint about 'the dull duties of a poet's trade' reflects Dryden's growing disenchantment with rhyme.
literary_significance: The last of Dryden's heroic plays and the point at which he turned away from rhyme toward blank verse in All for Love; it marks the end of the heroic drama's ascendancy.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1676. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vol. XIV (California).

title: All for Love; or, The World Well Lost
description: Dryden's rewriting of Antony and Cleopatra in blank verse, observing the unities of time, place, and action and confining itself to the last day in Alexandria; it is his own favourite among his plays.
plot_or_argument: After Actium, Antony refuses to fight Octavius again, is drawn into suspicion by Ventidius and Alexas, and Cleopatra feigns death; the lovers die together, and the world is 'well lost' for love.
narrative_structure: Five acts within the classical unities, with a single place (the temple of Isis at Alexandria) and a single day.
principal_characters: Marc Antony; Cleopatra; Ventidius; Alexas; Octavia; Serapion; Dolabella; Myris
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, written, Dryden said, 'in imitation of Shakespeare's style'; the prologue declares it the first play he ever wrote without rhyme.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1677 and published in 1678 with a preface defending the choice of blank verse and the observance of the unities.
literary_significance: The greatest heroic tragedy of the Restoration and the standard version of the Antony story on the English stage for more than a century; it remains Dryden's most frequently performed play.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1678. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vol. XV (California, 1996); All for Love (Monica M. Pearse, ed., New Mermaids).

title: Don Sebastian, King of Portugal
description: Dryden's last great tragedy, written after the Revolution of 1688, on the Portuguese king captured at Alcazarquivir, his enslavement in Morocco, and the discovery that the woman he loves is his own daughter.
plot_or_argument: Don Sebastian, presumed dead, is enslaved to the Mufti Moluch; he loves Almeyda, who is revealed as his sister's daughter and thus his own child; both renounce the world and retire to a monastery and a convent.
narrative_structure: Five acts combining a love tragedy with a political intrigue, ending in the tragic recognition of incest.
principal_characters: Don Sebastian; Almeyda; Muley Moluch; Dorax; Benducar; the Mufti; Johayma; Antonio
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1689 and published in 1690, after James II's flight and Dryden's loss of the laureateship for refusing the oaths to William and Mary.
literary_significance: Dryden's most complex late tragedy and a veiled meditation on fallen kingship and the legitimacy of allegiance; the character Dorax, a Portuguese renegade, is his finest creation after Almanzor.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1690. Standard edition: The Works of John Dryden, vol. XV (California).

title: King Arthur; or, The British Worthy
description: The Dryden-Purcell dramatic opera in five acts, celebrating Arthur's wars against the Saxons and his love for the blind Emmeline; it was originally conceived as a political allegory for the Exclusion Crisis and revived in the 1690s.
plot_or_argument: Arthur pursues the Saxon Oswald, who has stolen Emmeline; through enchantment, battles, and the restoration of Emmeline's sight, Arthur defeats the Saxons and unites Britain.
narrative_structure: Five acts with extensive music, masque episodes, and spectacular machinery; the spoken roles are limited to the principal characters.
principal_characters: King Arthur; Emmeline; Oswald; Merlin; Osmond; Philidel; Grimbald; Conon; Aurelius
meter_and_prosody: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
historical_context: Drafted in the 1680s as a Whig allegory of the Exclusion Crisis and rewritten for performance by the United Company at the Queen's Theatre, Dorset Garden, in June 1691 with music by Henry Purcell.
literary_significance: The greatest of the English semi-operas and the finest collaboration between a poet and a composer in the period; Purcell's score (including 'Fairest Isle' and the Frost Scene) is a landmark of English music.
attribution_notes: The text is by Dryden, the music by Purcell; the 1691 quarto names Dryden.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1691. Standard edition: King Arthur (John P. Loftis, ed., in The Works of John Dryden, California).

title: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
description: George Etherege's first comedy, a witty Restoration intrigue play that alternates heroic verse scenes of courtship with prose scenes of low comedy, and gave the stage its first true Restoration rake in Sir Frederick Frollick.
plot_or_argument: Two brothers love two sisters; Colonel Bruce and the Widow Rich clash in the main plot, while Sir Frederick Frollick pursues the Widow with comic irreverence; all is resolved in marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts with three parallel plots of differing social register and metre.
principal_characters: Sir Frederick Frollick; the Widow Rich; Colonel Bruce; Graciana; Beaufort; Palmer; Dufoy; Mrs Gudgeon
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed couplets in the high plot and prose in the low comedy.
historical_context: Performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1664; it made Etherege's reputation immediately.
literary_significance: The first of the great Restoration comedies of manners; Sir Frederick Frollick established the type of the gallant-rake that Dorimant would perfect.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1664. Standard edition: The Plays of Sir George Etherege (G. K. Hunter, ed., Oxford University Press, 1975).

title: She Would if She Could
description: Etherege's second comedy, a brilliant but famously unsuccessful intrigue play in which two rakes, Courtall and Sir Joslin Jolly, pursue two masked beauties through a series of crossed appointments.
plot_or_argument: Courtall and Sir Joslin arrange assignations with Ariana and Gatty; the women appear in disguise, the men are deceived, and a series of farcical failures leads to the marriages the title promises.
narrative_structure: Five acts of almost pure intrigue with a single day's action and minimal plot.
principal_characters: Courtall; Sir Joslin Jolly; Ariana; Gatty; Lady Cockwood; Rakehell; Mr Trim; Betty
meter_and_prosody: Sparkling prose throughout.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields on 6 February 1668 and failed with the audience, though Pepys admired it; it was long undervalued before the twentieth-century revival.
literary_significance: Now recognised as one of the finest and most formally daring Restoration comedies, its plotless brilliance anticipating Congreve.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1668. Standard edition: The Plays of Sir George Etherege (G. K. Hunter, ed., OUP, 1975).

title: The Man of Mode; or, Sir Fopling Flutter
description: Etherege's masterpiece, the greatest comedy of manners of the Restoration, in which the rake Dorimant manipulates a whole fashionable society of lovers, fops, and mothers with effortless wit.
plot_or_argument: Dorimant courts the rich heiress Harriet while abandoning Mrs Loveit; the fop Sir Fopling Flutter is mocked throughout; Dorimant wins Harriet by pretending to be a country gentleman, and the play ends with marriage and the rout of the pretenders.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intricate social intrigue with no subplot of consequence, unified by the figure of Dorimant.
principal_characters: Dorimant; Harriet; Mrs Loveit; Bellinda; Sir Fopling Flutter; Young Bellair; Emilia; Lady Woodvill; Medley; Shoat; Orange
meter_and_prosody: Prose of extraordinary rhythmic precision; the dialogue is the model of Restoration wit.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden on 11 March 1676 and dedicated to the Earl of Rochester; Dorimant was widely taken to be Rochester and Sir Fopling to be a caricature of several court fops.
literary_significance: The supreme achievement of Restoration social comedy and the model for Congreve, Sheridan, and Wilde; it created the type of the gentleman-rake and the standard of high-comic dialogue in English.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1676. Standard edition: The Plays of Sir George Etherege (G. K. Hunter, ed., OUP, 1975); The Man of Mode (Michael Cordner, ed., New Mermaids).

title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park
description: Wycherley's first comedy, a sprawling intrigue play set in St James's Park, in which masked gallants and ladies pursue one another through a series of night adventures.
plot_or_argument: Several couples are entangled in the fashionable world of the Park and the Exchange; disguises, duels, and betrayals are resolved in a set of marriages, with the virtuous Dapperwit exposed as a wit.
narrative_structure: Five acts with multiple plots and a low comic subplot of the city.
principal_characters: Ranger; Vincent; Lydia; Martha; Dapperwit; Mrs Crossbite; Alderman Gripe; Simon
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant with some verse.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1671 and published in 1672, dedicated to the Duchess of Cleveland.
literary_significance: An early and uneven but energetic comedy that anticipates Wycherley's later severity; its portrait of the Park is a valuable document of Restoration London.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1672. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of William Wycherley (Peter Holland, ed., Cambridge University Press, 1994).

title: The Gentleman Dancing-Master
description: Wycherley's second comedy, a satire on affectation of French and Spanish manners, in which a would-be Spanish grandee is fooled by his daughter's suitor disguised as a dancing master.
plot_or_argument: Monsieur de Parelle, an affecter of foreign fashions, is outwitted by St Jago, who courts his daughter Hippolita by posing as her dancing master; the plot exposes the emptiness of the gentleman's pretensions.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy with a strong comic central figure.
principal_characters: Monsieur de Parelle; Hippolita; St Jago; Madame Caution; Don Diego; Mrs Flareit
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1672 and published in 1673.
literary_significance: An important link between Wycherley's first comedy and his two masterpieces, notable for its satire on cultural affectation.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1673. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of William Wycherley (Peter Holland, ed., CUP, 1994).

title: The Country Wife
description: Wycherley's most famous comedy, in which Horner, a rake who pretends to have been unmanned by a surgeon, gains access to the wives and mistresses of the jealous town while the innocent country wife Margery is brought to London.
plot_or_argument: Horner's feigned impotence lets him seduce Lady Fidget, Mrs Squeamish, and others; the country wife Margery Pinchwife is kept under lock and key by her jealous husband, but her innocence defeats his vigilance; Horner's trick is nearly exposed and is saved by the women's complicity.
narrative_structure: Five acts with two parallel plots — Horner's intrigue and the Pinchwife marriage — and a low comic subplot of Sparkish and Alithea.
principal_characters: Horner; Margery Pinchwife; Mr Pinchwife; Lady Fidget; Alithea; Harcourt; Sparkish; Mrs Squeamish; Dorilant; Sir Jaspar Fidget
meter_and_prosody: Prose of great energy, with the famous china scene as the height of comic innuendo.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in January 1675 and published in the same year; it drew on Molière's L'École des femmes and L'École des maris.
literary_significance: The most performed and most discussed Restoration comedy; its savage exposure of jealousy, hypocrisy, and the marriage market makes it the darkest of the comedies of manners.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1675. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of William Wycherley (Peter Holland, ed., CUP, 1994); The Country Wife (James Ogden, ed., New Mermaids).

title: The Plain Dealer
description: Wycherley's second masterpiece, a bitter comedy of the blunt sea-captain Manly, who believes himself too honest for the world and is betrayed by his mistress, his friend, and his own self-deception.
plot_or_argument: Manly returns from sea to find his mistress Fidelia (disguised as a page) the only faithful soul; his friend Vernish steals his money and his mistress Olivia; Manly's rough justice exposes them and he marries Fidelia.
narrative_structure: Five acts, closely modelled on Molière's Le Misanthrope, with the low comic plot of Jerry Blackacre and the Widow Blackacre's lawsuit.
principal_characters: Manly; Fidelia; Vernish; Olivia; Eliza; Jerry Blackacre; the Widow Blackacre; Lord Plausible; Major Oldfox
meter_and_prosody: Prose, harsher and more rhetorical than in The Country Wife.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal on 11 December 1676 and published in 1677 with a dedication to the Duchess of Cleveland; Charles II is said to have rewarded Wycherley for it.
literary_significance: The bleakest and most psychologically complex of the Restoration comedies; Manly's misanthropy made the play a favourite of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and influenced Sheridan and Shaw.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1677. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of William Wycherley (Peter Holland, ed., CUP, 1994).

title: Epsom Wells
description: Thomas Shadwell's most popular comedy, set at the Epsom mineral wells, in which the fashionable world of gallants, cits, and country justices is exposed in a series of comic intrigues.
plot_or_argument: The rake Bellamour pursues Lucia while the city couple Woodly and Mrs Woodly play at adultery; the country justice Clodpate and his wife are gulled, and all is resolved in marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts of humours comedy with a strong Jonsonian comic portrait in Clodpate.
principal_characters: Bellamour; Woodly; Lucia; Carolina; Mrs Woodly; Justice Clodpate; Mrs Clodpate; Bumpkin; Lucy
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden in 1672 and published in 1673, dedicated to the Duke of Newcastle; Shadwell claimed to have drawn the characters from life at the wells.
literary_significance: Shadwell's finest comedy and a principal example of his Jonsonian 'humours' method; it held the stage into the eighteenth century through adaptation.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1673. Standard edition: The Complete Works of Thomas Shadwell (Montague Summers, ed., 1927).

title: The Virtuoso
description: Shadwell's comedy satirising the Royal Society and the new experimental philosophy through the figure of Sir Nicholas Gimcrack, an amateur scientist who wastes his fortune on absurd experiments.
plot_or_argument: Sir Nicholas pursues swimming-lessons for frogs and the extraction of air from cucumbers while his nieces and suitors conduct a normal intrigue; the satire is aimed not at science itself but at its pedantic misuse.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a Jonsonian comic central figure and a conventional love plot.
principal_characters: Sir Nicholas Gimcrack; Lady Gimcrack; Hazard; Longvil; Clara; Lucia; Mrs Figgup; Snarl; Sneak
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in May 1676 and published in the same year; Shadwell claimed to have attended Royal Society meetings for two years to get his material, and the portrait was taken as an attack on the Society's Fellows.
literary_significance: The most important dramatic satire on the early Royal Society and a key text in the history of the quarrel between the wits and the philosophers; Gimcrack became a byword for the foolish virtuoso.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1676. Standard edition: The Complete Works of Thomas Shadwell (Montague Summers, ed., 1927).

title: The Squire of Alsatia
description: Shadwell's late comedy, set in the Whitefriars district known as Alsatia, a sanctuary for debtors and criminals, in which the innocent young Belfond senior is corrupted by the cheats of the place.
plot_or_argument: Two brothers are raised in strict ignorance by their father; the elder is taken into Alsatia and ruined by its rogues, while the younger, Shamwell, survives; the plot exposes a whole gallery of swindlers.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a strongly topographical Jonsonian comic method.
principal_characters: Belfond senior; Belfond junior (Shamwell); Sir William Belfond; Cheatly; Captain Teresia; Abraham Cow; Mrs Termagant; Laure
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1688, shortly before the Revolution; Shadwell was Poet Laureate and Historiographer Royal from 1689 until his death in 1692.
literary_significance: Shadwell's most ambitious late comedy and his fullest study of London criminal topography; 'Alsatia' entered the language as a word for a lawless district.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1688. Standard edition: The Complete Works of Thomas Shadwell (Montague Summers, ed., 1927).

title: The Rival Queens; or, The Death of Alexander the Great
description: Nathaniel Lee's wildly popular heroic tragedy on the death of Alexander, driven by the rivalry between his two wives, Roxana and Statira; it was the most performed play of the Restoration and a byword for bombast.
plot_or_argument: Alexander returns to Babylon to find Roxana mad with jealousy of Statira; the conspiracy of Cassander, Perdiccas, and others breaks out, Alexander is poisoned, and Roxana kills Statira before being carried off in triumph.
narrative_structure: Five acts of high heroic tragedy with two rival women at the centre.
principal_characters: Alexander the Great; Roxana; Statira; Cassander; Perdiccas; Lysimachus; Hephaestion; Thessalus
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of extravagant rhetorical height, famously parodying the heroic style.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in March 1677 and published the same year; it held the stage for over a century and was parodied by Fielding and in The Rehearsal tradition.
literary_significance: The most successful Restoration tragedy after All for Love and the standard example of the excesses of the heroic drama; its 'rival queens' structure influenced the eighteenth-century she-tragedy.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1677. Standard edition: The Works of Nathaniel Lee (T. H. Montague, ed., 1954).

title: Sophonisba; or, Hannibal's Overthrow
description: Lee's early heroic tragedy on the Carthaginian princess Sophonisba, who drinks poison rather than fall into Roman hands, and whose lines 'O happiness! O pleasure!' became proverbial for heroic bombast.
plot_or_argument: Sophonisba, betrothed to Massinissa, is captured by the Romans; to save her from their triumph she takes poison given by Massinissa, and Hannibal's cause collapses.
narrative_structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single tragic action.
principal_characters: Sophonisba; Massinissa; Hannibal; Syphax; Scipio; Melbo; Narbal
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of high rhetorical strain.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676; it was one of the earliest plays in which the young actor Thomas Betterton shone in a heroic role.
literary_significance: An important early heroic tragedy and the source of some of the most frequently quoted lines of Restoration bombast; it establishes Lee's reputation before The Rival Queens.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1676. Standard edition: The Works of Nathaniel Lee (T. H. Montague, ed., 1954).

title: Lucius Junius Brutus, Father of His Country
description: Lee's republican tragedy on the expulsion of the Tarquins and the founding of the Roman republic, banned by the Lord Chamberlain in 1680 for its allegedly republican politics.
plot_or_argument: Brutus feigns idiocy under the tyrant Tarquin; after the rape of Lucretia he leads the revolt, and sacrifices his own sons for treason rather than betray the new republic.
narrative_structure: Five acts of political tragedy culminating in the hero's filial sacrifice.
principal_characters: Lucius Junius Brutus; Tarquin; Lucretia; Teraminta; Titus; Tiberius; Collatinus; Herminius
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse.
historical_context: Prohibited from performance in 1680 by the Lord Chamberlain on the ground that it contained 'very scandalous expressions and reflections upon monarchical government'; printed in 1681 during the Exclusion Crisis.
literary_significance: An important document of Whig political sentiment in the drama and a forerunner of the eighteenth-century republican tragedies of Addison and Thomson; its suppression is a classic case of Restoration censorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1681. Standard edition: The Works of Nathaniel Lee (T. H. Montague, ed., 1954).
